questions.prompt: A $400\text{-kg}$ satellite has been placed in a circular orbit $1500\,\text{km}$ above the surface of the earth. The acceleration of gravity at this elevation is $6.43\,\text{m/s}^2$. Determine the magnitude of the linear momentum of the satellite, knowing that its orbital speed is $25.6 \times 10^3\,\text{km/h}$ (in $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$).
questions.solution:
Linear momentum $L = mv$ uses the **mass**, which does not depend on the local value of $g$ (the $6.43\,\text{m/s}^2$ is a distractor).

$v = \dfrac{25.6 \times 10^6\,\text{m}}{3600\,\text{s}} = 7111\,\text{m/s}$.

$L = (400\,\text{kg})(7111\,\text{m/s}) = 2.84 \times 10^6\,\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$.

questions.prompt: A spring scale is fastened to the roof of an elevator and a package hangs from it. When the elevator moves **downward** with an acceleration of $1\,\text{m/s}^2$, the spring scale indicates a load of $60\,\text{N}$. Determine the weight of the package (in $\text{N}$).
questions.solution:
The scale reading is the force $F$ it exerts on the package. Positive downward: $\sum F = ma$: $mg - F = m(1) \Rightarrow 60 = m(9.81 - 1) \Rightarrow m = 6.81\,\text{kg}$.

$W = mg = 6.81(9.81) = 66.8\,\text{N}$.

questions.prompt: A spring scale $A$ and a lever scale $B$ having equal lever arms are fastened to the roof of an elevator, with identical packages attached. When the elevator moves downward with $a = 1\,\text{m/s}^2$ the spring scale reads $60\,\text{N}$. When the elevator moves **upward** with $a = 1\,\text{m/s}^2$, what are the load indicated by the spring scale and the mass needed to balance the lever scale?
questions.solution:
From the downward case, $m = 60/(9.81 - 1) = 6.81\,\text{kg}$.

Upward acceleration, positive up: $F - mg = ma \Rightarrow F = m(g + a) = 6.81(10.81) = 73.6\,\text{N}$.

The lever scale compares two masses subject to the **same** acceleration, so the balancing mass equals the package mass, $6.81\,\text{kg}$, whatever the elevator's acceleration.

questions.prompt: An automobile's braking distance from $90\,\text{km/h}$ is $45\,\text{m}$ on level pavement. Assuming the braking force is independent of grade, determine the braking distance from $90\,\text{km/h}$ when it is going **up** a $5^\circ$ incline (in $\text{m}$).
questions.solution:
$v_0 = 90\,\text{km/h} = 25\,\text{m/s}$. Level: $0 = v_0^2 - 2a_0(45) \Rightarrow a_0 = \dfrac{625}{90} = 6.944\,\text{m/s}^2$, so the braking force is $F_b = m(6.944)$.

Up the incline, both $F_b$ and the weight component oppose the motion: $\sum F = ma$: $-F_b - mg\sin 5^\circ = ma \Rightarrow a = -(6.944 + 9.81\sin 5^\circ) = -7.799\,\text{m/s}^2$.

$d = \dfrac{v_0^2}{2|a|} = \dfrac{625}{2(7.799)} = 40.1\,\text{m}$.

questions.prompt: An automobile's braking distance from $90\,\text{km/h}$ is $45\,\text{m}$ on level pavement. Assuming the braking force is independent of grade, determine the braking distance from $90\,\text{km/h}$ when it is going **down** a 3-percent incline (in $\text{m}$).
questions.solution:
As in part (a), $F_b = m(6.944\,\text{m/s}^2)$. A 3-percent grade has $\tan\theta = 0.03$, $\theta = 1.718^\circ$, $\sin\theta = 0.0300$.

Going down, the weight component aids the motion: $a = -(6.944 - 9.81 \times 0.0300) = -6.650\,\text{m/s}^2$.

$d = \dfrac{625}{2(6.650)} = 47.0\,\text{m}$.

questions.prompt: A mother holds a rope tied to her $20\text{-kg}$ child's waist. They are moving at $7.2\,\text{km/h}$ on a slope inclined at $5^\circ$ when she pulls on the rope with an average force of $7\,\text{N}$ (rope at $20^\circ$ to the horizontal, as shown). Knowing the coefficient of friction between the child and the ground is $0.1$ and the angle of the rope does not change, determine the time required for the child's speed to be cut in half (in $\text{s}$).
questions.solution:
$v_0 = 7.2\,\text{km/h} = 2\,\text{m/s}$. Axes: $x$ down the $5^\circ$ slope, $y$ normal to it. The rope pulls up the slope at $20^\circ - 5^\circ = 15^\circ$ to the slope surface.

$\sum F_y = 0$: $N = mg\cos 5^\circ - 7\sin 15^\circ = 195.45 - 1.81 = 193.64\,\text{N}$; friction $F = 0.1N = 19.36\,\text{N}$ up the slope.

$\sum F_x = ma$: $mg\sin 5^\circ - 7\cos 15^\circ - 19.36 = 20a \Rightarrow 17.10 - 6.76 - 19.36 = 20a \Rightarrow a = -0.451\,\text{m/s}^2$.

Speed halves ($2 \to 1\,\text{m/s}$): $t = \dfrac{1 - 2}{-0.451} = 2.22\,\text{s}$.

questions.prompt: For the mother-and-child skiing situation shown ($20\text{-kg}$ child, initial speed $7.2\,\text{km/h}$, $5^\circ$ slope, $7\text{-N}$ rope pull at $20^\circ$ to the horizontal, coefficient of friction $0.1$), determine the distance traveled by the child while its speed is cut in half (in $\text{m}$).
questions.solution:
From the equations of motion (see part a), the constant acceleration is $a = -0.451\,\text{m/s}^2$.

$v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\,\Delta x$: $1^2 = 2^2 + 2(-0.451)\Delta x \Rightarrow \Delta x = \dfrac{3}{0.902} = 3.32\,\text{m}$.

questions.prompt: The coefficients of friction between the load and the flatbed trailer shown are $\mu_s = 0.40$ and $\mu_k = 0.30$. Knowing that the speed of the rig is $72\,\text{km/h}$, determine the shortest distance in which the rig can be brought to a stop if the load is not to shift (in $\text{m}$).
questions.solution:
If the load does not shift, it has the rig's deceleration, provided by static friction: $F = ma \le \mu_s N = \mu_s mg$, so $a_{\max} = \mu_s g = 0.40(9.81) = 3.924\,\text{m/s}^2$.

$v_0 = 72\,\text{km/h} = 20\,\text{m/s}$: $d_{\min} = \dfrac{v_0^2}{2a_{\max}} = \dfrac{400}{7.848} = 51.0\,\text{m}$.

questions.prompt: A light train made up of two cars is traveling at $90\,\text{km/h}$ when the brakes are applied to both cars. Car $A$ has a mass of $25\,\text{Mg}$ and car $B$ a mass of $20\,\text{Mg}$, and the braking force is $30\,\text{kN}$ on each car. Determine the distance traveled by the train before it comes to a stop (in $\text{m}$).

For the two-car train shown ($m_A = 25\,\text{Mg}$ leading, $m_B = 20\,\text{Mg}$, braking force $30\,\text{kN}$ on each car, initial speed $90\,\text{km/h}$), what is the force in the coupling between the cars while the train is slowing down?

options.label: D
options.text: Zero, since both cars are braked

questions.solution:
Train deceleration: $a = 60\,000/45\,000 = 1.333\,\text{m/s}^2$.

Car $A$ alone needs a retarding force $m_Aa = 25\,000(1.333) = 33.33\,\text{kN}$ but its brakes supply only $30\,\text{kN}$; the remaining $3.33\,\text{kN}$ must be supplied by the coupling pulling $A$ backward — the coupling is in **tension**.

Check with car $B$: it needs $20\,000(1.333) = 26.67\,\text{kN}$ but its brakes give $30\,\text{kN}$, so the coupling pulls it forward with $3.33\,\text{kN}$.

questions.prompt: An airplane has a mass of $25\,\text{Mg}$ and its engines develop a total thrust of $40\,\text{kN}$ during take-off. The drag on the plane is $D = 2.25v^2$ ($D$ in newtons, $v$ in m/s). If the plane becomes airborne at a speed of $240\,\text{km/h}$, determine the length of runway required (in $\text{m}$).

The horizontal rod $OA$ rotates about a vertical shaft according to $\dot\theta = 10t$ (rad/s, s). A $250\text{-g}$ collar $B$ is held by a cord with a breaking strength of $18\,\text{N}$. Neglecting friction, determine the magnitude of the relative acceleration of the collar with respect to the rod immediately after the cord breaks (in $\text{m/s}^2$).
questions.solution:
Before the break the collar is at fixed $r$ ($\dot r = \ddot r = 0$) and the cord supplies the radial force: $-T = m(\ddot r - r\dot\theta^2) = -mr\dot\theta^2$. The cord breaks when $T = 18\,\text{N}$, i.e. when $r\dot\theta^2 = 18/0.25 = 72\,\text{m/s}^2$.

Immediately after the break there is no radial force (the frictionless rod exerts only a transverse force): $0 = m(\ddot r - r\dot\theta^2) \Rightarrow \ddot r = r\dot\theta^2 = 72.0\,\text{m/s}^2$.

The acceleration relative to the rod is $\ddot r = 72.0\,\text{m/s}^2$, radially outward.

questions.prompt: The moon completes one revolution about the earth in $\tau = 27.3$ days. Using $g = 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$ and $R = 6370\,\text{km}$ for the earth, and treating the orbit as circular, compute the radius $r$ of the moon's orbit (in $\text{km}$).
questions.solution:
Circular orbit: $\dfrac{GMm}{r^2} = m\dfrac{v^2}{r}$ with $v = 2\pi r/\tau$, so $r^3 = \dfrac{GM\tau^2}{4\pi^2} = \dfrac{gR^2\tau^2}{4\pi^2}$.

$gR^2 = 9.81(6.37 \times 10^6)^2 = 398.1 \times 10^{12}\,\text{m}^3/\text{s}^2$; $\tau = 27.3(86\,400) = 2.359 \times 10^6\,\text{s}$.

$r^3 = \dfrac{(398.1 \times 10^{12})(2.359 \times 10^6)^2}{39.48} = 56.1 \times 10^{24}\,\text{m}^3 \Rightarrow r = 383 \times 10^6\,\text{m} = 383 \times 10^3\,\text{km}$.

questions.prompt: A $500\text{-kg}$ spacecraft is placed into a circular orbit about the earth at an altitude of $4500\,\text{km}$. Determine the gravitational force exerted on the spacecraft in that orbit (in $\text{N}$). Use $R = 6370\,\text{km}$, $g = 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$.

A spacecraft in a circular earth orbit at an altitude of $4500\,\text{km}$ ($R_{\text{earth}} = 6370\,\text{km}$) is transferred to a circular orbit about the moon. The mass of the moon is $0.01230$ times the mass of the earth. Determine the radius of the orbit about the moon if the periodic times of the two orbits are to be equal (in $\text{km}$).
questions.solution:
For a circular orbit $\tau = \dfrac{2\pi r^{3/2}}{\sqrt{GM}}$. Equal periods: $\dfrac{r_m^3}{M_m} = \dfrac{r_e^3}{M_e}$.

$r_e = 10\,870\,\text{km}$: $r_m = r_e\Big(\dfrac{M_m}{M_e}\Big)^{1/3} = 10\,870(0.01230)^{1/3} = 10\,870(0.2308) = 2510\,\text{km}$.

questions.prompt: The mass of the moon is $0.01230$ times the mass of the earth and the radius of the moon is $1737\,\text{km}$. Using $g = 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$ and $R = 6370\,\text{km}$ for the earth, determine the acceleration of gravity at the surface of the moon (in $\text{m/s}^2$).
